/-!
# Magic Squares

*References:*

* [Magic Square of Squares - Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magic_square_of_squares)
* [multimagie.com](http://www.multimagie.com/English/SquaresOfSquaresSearch.htm)
* [Semi-Magic Square of Cubes](https://unsolvedproblems.org/index_files/SquareofCubes.htm)
* [Magic Square of Squares](https://static.nsta.org/pdfs/QuantumV6N3.pdf)
-/

@[expose] public section

namespace MagicSquares

/--
Does there exist a $3 \times 3$ matrix such that every entry is a distinct square,
and all rows, columns, and diagonals add up to the same value?

0 is excluded, as a Magic Square of Squares with 0 and 8 distinct squares is know is knownn.
See [Magic Square of Squares](https://static.nsta.org/pdfs/QuantumV6N3.pdf)
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem exists_magic_square_squares :
    answer(sorry) ↔ ∃ m : Fin 3 → Fin 3 → ℕ, ∃ t : ℕ,
       m.Injective2 ∧
       (∀ i j, 0 < (m i j) ∧ IsSquare (m i j)) ∧
       (∀ i, ∑ j, m i j = t) ∧
       (∀ j, ∑ i, m i j = t) ∧
       m 0 0 + m 1 1 + m 2 2 = t ∧
       m 0 2 + m 1 1 + m 2 0 = t := by
  sorry

/--
Does there exist a $3 \times 3$ semi-magic square whose entries are all distinct positive
integer cubes? A square is semi-magic if all rows and columns sum to the same total.

More precisely, we seek a $3 \times 3$ matrix with entries $a_{ij}$ such that each
$a_{ij} = n_{ij}^3$ for some positive integer $n_{ij}$, all nine cubes are distinct,
and all row sums and column sums are equal.

*Reference:*
[Semi-Magic Square of Cubes](https://unsolvedproblems.org/index_files/SquareofCubes.htm)
-/
@[category research open, AMS 5 11]
theorem exists_semi_magic_square_cubes :
    answer(sorry) ↔ ∃ m : Fin 3 → Fin 3 → ℕ, ∃ t : ℕ,
       m.Injective2 ∧
       (∀ i j, ∃ n : ℕ, 0 < n ∧ m i j = n ^ 3) ∧
       (∀ i, ∑ j, m i j = t) ∧
       (∀ j, ∑ i, m i j = t) := by
  sorry

end MagicSquares

findings.description: The docstring at line 39 incorrectly says that a magic square with zero and eight distinct square entries is known. This repeats a subsequently corrected error in Gardner's January 1996 article: those examples are only semi-magic, not magic on both diagonals as this declaration requires. In fact, a fully magic 3×3 square of distinct natural-number squares cannot contain zero. The Lean statement itself is faithful; only the explanation for excluding zero is erroneous.
findings.source_evidence: The cited January article, Quantum 6(3), p. 25 (https://static.nsta.org/pdfs/QuantumV6N3.pdf), does make this claim. However, Gardner explicitly corrects it in “The latest magic,” Quantum 6(4), March/April 1996, p. 60: “In my article I said that order-3 squares made of squares are possible with zero in one cell. I should have added that squares of this type are magic only in rows and columns.” https://static.nsta.org/pdfs/QuantumV6N4.pdf
findings.suggested_fix: Remove the claimed known zero-containing magic square. Either simply state that the entries are positive integer squares, or explain that positivity follows from the other conditions. If mentioning the known zero-containing examples, identify them as semi-magic and cite Gardner's correction. No change to the Lean theorem statement is needed.

reformulations.difference: The Lean statement explicitly requires every square entry to be positive, whereas the source's question about nine distinct integer squares does not need a separate exclusion of zero.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: In a 3×3 magic square with centre e and common total t, the line equations imply t = 3e and that opposite entries sum to 2e. Nonnegative entries and distinctness force e > 0. If any other entry were zero, its opposite would be 2e. Writing e = b² and the opposite entry as a² would give a² = 2b² with b > 0, which is impossible. Hence all entries are automatically positive. The exact equivalence between the theorem's right-hand side and the version without positivity was proved as magic_squares_positive_iff in /workspace/review/equivalence.lean, without sorry.

sources_consulted: https://static.nsta.org/pdfs/QuantumV6N3.pdf — Martin Gardner, “The magic of 3×3,” Quantum 6(3), pp. 24–26
https://static.nsta.org/pdfs/QuantumV6N4.pdf — Martin Gardner, “The latest magic,” Quantum 6(4), p. 60
http://www.multimagie.com/English/SquaresOfSquares.htm — introduction to Christian Boyer's 2005 article and open-problem discussion
review.notes: Both theorem statements faithfully encode their cited existence questions, and the consulted sources continue to record both problems as open. Checked answer-slot scope and polarity, global distinctness via Injective2, square/cube semantics, all required line sums, and zero/constant boundary cases. Scratch Lean checks compiled successfully, including tests of the sources' near-miss examples and the positivity equivalence. No repository files were edited.
